prompt:
[quiet, slow] My grandmother used to say: if someone calls your name at night, don't answer. Your own can wait till morning.

[quiet, tired] I thought it was just something you tell kids so they don't stay out after dark.

The Horizon business center closed a month ago. The building was up for sale, but someone still had to guard it at night.

Night shifts paid double. And my sister needed something to live on in a strange city.

[quiet, warm] My lock screen was a drawing Lily made: the three of us, me, her and our dog Biscuit. She was six.

[quiet, tired] The day guard was waiting for me by the turnstile. He'd put his jacket on before I even walked in.

[casual] Yeah. What happened to Frank?

[curious] What do you mean, never handed it over?

[quiet, tired] The keys were warm. He hadn't let go of them all evening.

Out on the street he rapped his knuckles on the glass. Three times. He looked at me as if he wanted to say something else. He didn't.

[quiet, tired] The first hours were quiet: rounds, tea, monitors. I didn't sit down with the logbook until ten to three.

Frank's handwriting was small and even, as if he'd used a ruler. Twenty years of the same entries: rounds, lamps, the cat by the dumpsters.

[quiet, reading] October twelfth. "The elevator runs by itself at night. The technician says it's a sensor."

The fifteenth. "Someone calls Gus from the seventh floor. By name. In Martha's voice. Martha's been dead three years."

The eighteenth. "A thirteenth camera showed up on the console. There's no such camera in the building. Don't look at it."

[quiet, uneasy] The twentieth. Here he'd pressed so hard the pen tore the paper. "Don't answer to your name. Don't open the door to it. And don't go to it yourself, not to the light, not into the elevator. Then it can't come near you."

The twenty-first. The last entry, the handwriting no longer even. "Mom called. I answered. Salt holds it. Going down."

[quiet, tired] I decided the old man had lost his mind. Twenty years of night shifts — anyone would crack.

[quiet, tense] At one minute to three, the lights came on on the seventh floor.

[quiet, tired] The entrance. Empty. Just rain.

[quiet, tense] Someone by the elevator?.. No. Just the shadow of the potted palm.

[quiet, relieved] Seven. A cleaner mopping the floor. So I'm not alone here.

[casual] Copy. I'm the new guy, first shift.

[quiet, tense] At exactly three, Gus stopped humming. He straightened up and turned to the door of seven-oh-seven. As if someone had called him.

The radio hissed: he'd pressed the button by accident.

[quiet, shaken] The picture broke into static. When it came back, there was only a bucket and a mop in the corridor.

I watched the recording three times. At that second, the door of seven-oh-seven was closed. And Gus was talking to it.

[quiet, bitter] I called the police. The officer asked if there was a body. There wasn't. "His family can file a report in the morning."

[quiet, tense] Leave? The doors were across the whole lobby, past the elevator. By Frank's rules, the booth was safer.

[quiet, tired] The seventh floor stayed lit and empty. I sat there staring at the bucket.

[whispering, cold] Gus didn't know my name. I never told him.

[quiet, tense] A minute later the elevator came down to the lobby. Nobody had called it.

The display above the doors said thirteen. The Horizon has twelve floors.

The doors stood open for a while. Then closed on their own.

The display went dark. And camera thirteen came on on the console.

[whispering, terrified] A long corridor that doesn't exist in this building. At the end of it, someone with their back to me.

[quiet, tired] I yanked the cord. For ten minutes I sat in the dark, listening to the empty building hum.

[quiet, slow] Don't answer. Don't open. I kept repeating it to myself until the words stopped meaning anything.

[quiet, tense] At half past three, someone outside called my name.

[quiet, stunned] Lily was standing outside the glass. In her yellow sweater, in the rain.

[quiet, confused] She was supposed to be asleep in her dorm. Two hundred miles from here.

[whispering, terrified] I glanced at the entrance monitor. Where she was standing, there was nothing but static.

My phone buzzed. A message from Lily. Sent a minute ago. From the phone that had "died."

Rain was streaming down the glass, and she was pressing her face against it. The glass only fogged up on my side.

With my finger I wrote on the fogged glass: "What was our dog's name?" She didn't even glance at the letters.

Biscuit. Lily named him herself. And this thing just kept repeating my name. The same voice. The same intonation.

I stepped back from the door.

[quiet, hesitant] I turned the key.

[quiet, emotional] She threw her arms around my neck. Ice-cold, soaked through.

[gentle, comforting] It's okay, it's okay. You're here now. You're with me.

[quiet, uneasy] She stopped crying. Instantly. As if someone had hit mute.

[whispering, terrified] She didn't smell like rain. She smelled of machine oil and dust. Like an elevator shaft.

My phone rang. The screen said: "Lily."

Lily was standing right next to me. Her hands were empty. And the phone kept ringing.

I looked up. The lobby was empty. Just wet footprints, leading to the elevator.

The elevator went up. Five. Nine. Twelve. Thirteen.

Monitor thirteen turned on by itself, with its cord pulled out. At the end of the corridor, a yellow sweater. It slowly turned around.

It wasn't her face. And it was smiling into the camera.

[quiet, despair] Frank had warned me. And I opened the door myself. Let it in myself.

[whispering, terrified] The elevator started down.

I locked the booth. Switched off the lamp. Slid down to the floor under the counter.

[whispering, terrified] The elevator doors. Footsteps. Bare, wet. Closer.

The phone in my pocket vibrated. I covered it with my hand. Too late.

[whispering, exhausted] The footsteps circled the booth. An hour. Then another.

[whispering, hollow] At one minute to six she called again, in a whisper. And I answered before I realized I was answering.

[quiet, hollow] At six the front door banged. The day guard had arrived.

He looked at me. And backed away. Slowly, without turning his back.

[quiet, hollow, eerie] I saw my reflection in the booth glass. I was smiling. Wider than I know how. And I wasn't blinking.

[tense, breathless] The emergency exit was at the end of the service corridor. Forty steps.

The lights went out behind me: it was following the sound of my steps.

[breathless] I tumbled out into the rain and ran until I couldn't breathe.

[quiet, breathless] The Horizon stood dark. Only above the roof, where there are no more floors, a window was lit.

[quiet] My phone rang. Lily.

[whispering, terrified] I was standing in the rain outside the Horizon. Two hundred miles from her window.

I didn't open it. She stopped crying. Instantly.

And smiled. Too wide. Lily never smiled like that.

She scraped the glass with her nails. Slowly, top to bottom.

Then she left. Walking backwards. Never taking her eyes off me.

Rain streamed down the glass, but the print of her palm didn't wash away.

[quiet, tense] I called Lily. One ring. Two. Three.

[tense] Where are you right now?

[gentle, serious] Everything's fine. Go back to sleep. Just, if someone calls your name tonight, don't answer. Even if it's me.

[quiet, tired] I hung up. My hands were shaking.

[whispering, terrified] I'd pulled the cord on thirteen an hour ago. The monitor turned on anyway.

The seventh floor. Gus had turned up. He was lying in the doorway of seven-oh-seven.

[whispering, terrified] It was crouched over him. Low, right at his chest. Taking its time.

It started to raise its head toward the lens. I squeezed my eyes shut.

[quiet, tense] When I opened my eyes, thirteen was dark. And on the next monitor the server-room camera had come to life. It had been black all night. Now a candle was burning.

[quiet, stunned] Basement two. A circle of salt on the floor. A man sitting inside it. The face from the ID badge above my desk. Frank. Alive. Gaunt, unshaven.

[quiet, bitter] They'd searched twelve floors. Nobody thought of the basement.

[quiet, tense] He held a crumpled sheet up to the camera. The letters traced over and over. He must have been showing it every night.

[whispering, terrified] Frank suddenly looked back into the dark. As if someone had called him.

[quiet, tense] I didn't touch the elevator. The stairs. Basement one. Basement two.

[whispering, terrified] It smelled of damp and wax. Salt crunched underfoot.

An iron door. "Server Room." A strip of warm light underneath it.

[whispering, terrified] An old man's voice. Maybe that's what Frank sounded like. Except Frank had never heard my name.

And the sheet had said: "Don't call me. Knock three times."

I knocked. Once. Twice. Three times.

Silence. Then the bolt clanked. From the inside.

[quiet] Frank had poured his circle right at the threshold: he could reach the bolt without leaving the salt. One of his legs was taped to a piece of cardboard.

[whispering, terrified] From the dark beyond the circle, someone called to Frank. An old woman's voice. Tender.

Frank reached toward the voice. Toward the edge of the circle.

[quiet, exhausted] At six, the voice broke off mid-word.

[quiet, tired] I put his arm over my shoulder. Forty steps up. He didn't say a word.

[quiet, calm] We stepped out into the rain. It wasn't light yet. But somewhere behind the houses the first tram had already gone by.

[quiet] I shook my head.

Frank lit a cigarette.

[quiet, tired] I didn't leave. Lily needed the money.

[quiet, slow] Now every night, at exactly three, someone stands by the elevator and calls my name. In Lily's voice. So far, I haven't answered once.

[quiet, tired] I didn't go anywhere. It could have been anyone. Anything.

For an hour and a half I watched the monitors. Thirteen didn't come on again.

[quiet, guilty] Somewhere beneath me, an old man sat in a circle of salt. And I sat upstairs, waiting for six.

[quiet, tense] At five-forty my phone rang. "Lily."

[whispering] Twenty minutes to six. Your own can wait till morning.

[quiet, tense] I declined. It called again. And again. Then it went quiet.

[quiet, tired] At six the day guard came in.

[quiet, hollow] We went down together. The server-room door was wide open. Handprints trailed from the circle out into the corridor.

[quiet, slow] I opened the logbook to the last page and added a line. In my own handwriting. For whoever comes after me.

[whispering, terrified] I looked at thirteen. It was already facing the camera. As if it had been waiting for me to look.

It said my name. And I answered before I realized I was answering.

[quiet, tense] I went up to seven. The lights were on. It smelled of a wet rag.

[whispering, terrified] Gus was lying in the doorway of seven-oh-seven. Someone was crouched over him.

The lights started going out. From the far end. Toward me.

[urgent, loud] Gus! Hang on, I'm coming up!

[whispering, terrified] I wasn't fast enough. The one in the corridor turned around. It had no face. Only a mouth. And the mouth said my name.

And I answered before I realized I was answering.

[quiet, tense] I opened the door.

[whispering, terrified] Frank was sitting in the circle. Looking at me and shaking his head: no, no, no.

And the voice that had called me was right behind me.

Frank crawled out of the circle. The dark closed over him without a sound.

[urgent, scared] Frank?!

[whispering, terrified] It was her voice. But it wasn't coming from the phone. It was coming from the lobby.

[gruff, in a hurry] You the new guy? Frank's replacement?

[gruff, uneasy] Frank sat in that booth for twenty years. A week ago he never handed over his shift.

[low, uneasy] In the morning the booth's open, the lamp's on, the tea's gone cold. His jacket's on the chair. And no Frank.

The police went through all twelve floors. The cameras didn't catch a thing.

[low, serious] The logbook's on the desk. Read it before three. All of it, to the last page.

[low, wary] You didn't answer?

You didn't answer?

[friendly, old man] Security, come in. This is Gus, the cleaner. I'm on seven, I'll be done by four. I'm on the radio if you need me.

[tender, confused] Martha?.. Is that you?

[weak, pleading] Security… Ethan, can you hear me? I'm stuck in the elevator, between floors… Ethan, answer me…

[calm, warm, creepy] Thank you, Ethan.

[crying, desperate] Ethan! Ethan, open the door, please!

[crying, shivering] I wanted to surprise you… My phone died, I walked from the station. Ethan, I'm freezing!

[panicked, scared] Ethan, someone's coming! Open the door!

[flat, sweet, creepy] Ethan… Open up. I'm cold. Ethan.

[whispering, sweet, creepy] Ethan… Are you here? Come on, take a breath.

[sleepy, puzzled] Ethan? Why did you call? You said you were standing under my window…

[whispering, scared] Ethan… then who's calling me from the street? In your voice.

[flat, monotone, creepy] Ethan. Ethan. Ethan.

[sleepy] Mm… Ethan? It's half past three… What happened?

[sleepy, worried] In the dorm, where else. Sleeping. Ethan, you're scaring me.

[whispering, sweet, creepy] There you are, Ethan.

[calm, sweet, creepy] Ethan. Finally.

[whispering, distant, creepy] Ethan…

[hoarse, kind, old man] Ethan? That you, son? Come on in, it's open.

[whispering, urgent, old man] Inside. Quick. And not a sound.

[hoarse, tired, old man] Fell on the stairs a week ago. Crawled down here. Water cooler, crackers from the emergency cabinet. In the daytime I shouted. Nobody hears through that door.

Held out six nights. Can't make it through the seventh alone.

[hoarse, grim, old man] Only the salt holds me now. And the only thing holding you is keeping your mouth shut.

[quiet, almost joyful] Mom?..

[hoarse, exhausted, old man] That's it. It sleeps till nightfall.

[quiet, old man] Gus?

[quiet, sad, old man] That's why he kept coming here, you know. To listen to her.

[quiet, bitter, old man] Wrote it down myself: don't answer. And the very next night Mom called, and I answered. Buried her thirty years ago.

[quiet, grave, old man] Now I sleep in a circle for the rest of my life. But you get out of here, son. Before you answer.

[quiet, old man, distant] Ethan?..
